title: When and How SignSGD Outperforms SGD: A Functional Scaling Law Perspective
claim: A noise-aware scaling law predicts training dynamics and shows the sign-based optimizer scales better with data and tolerates larger batches.
layout: 3 panels in a row, left-to-right, orange vs blue color coding
description: Three line plots side by side with a shared orange and blue palette. The left panel, titled 'Risk dynamics', plots risk against step (up to 10k). It shows noisy trajectories for cosine, WSD and cyclic learning-rate schedules, with smooth theory curves overlaid on the noisy runs. The middle panel, titled 'Data scaling', is a log-log plot of final risk against data budget. Two dashed power-law lines show SignSGD (blue) falling more steeply than SGD (orange). The right panel, titled 'Critical batch size', plots normalized risk against batch size on log axes. SGD (orange) rises above a dashed 1.2x threshold line at a batch size of about 16. SignSGD (blue) stays flat until about 2000. Arrows and annotations mark the two critical batch sizes. The eye goes first to the colored curves and the annotated arrows in the right panel.
caption: SignSGD FSL accurately captures risk dynamics and predicts scaling behavior. (Left) FSL predictions track SignSGD risk trajectories under cosine, WSD, and cyclic LR schedules. (Middle) In the hard-task regime, SignSGD achieves a larger data-scaling exponent than SGD, $\gamma_{\sgn}>\gamma_{\sgd}$ in $\cE(D)\eqsim D^{-\gamma}$, indicating improved data efficiency. Dashed lines denote power-law fits. (Right) In the easy-task regime, SignSGD improves step efficiency through a larger CBS, requiring fewer optimization steps at a fixed data budget while preserving small-batch performance. Risk is normalized by each optimizer's $B=1$ baseline. Marked CBS estimates use a $20%$ risk-increase tolerance.
abstract: We study how the sign operator interacts with gradient noise to shape the learning dynamics and scaling behavior of sign-based optimizers. In power-law kernel regression with diagonal features, we establish a functional scaling law (FSL) for SignSGD under general learning rate schedules. The FSL describes the learning dynamics through two processes: signal learning and noise forgetting. The key mechanism is noise-induced preconditioning: gradient noise smooths the sign operator, inducing an effective preconditioned SGD. Noise-curvature alignment enables this preconditioning to transform the effective Hessian from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{H}^{1/2}$. The resulting dynamics exhibit faster signal learning but slower noise forgetting than SGD. This tradeoff yields a regime-dependent comparison with SGD: (i) SignSGD achieves improved data efficiency in the hard-task regime; (ii) both optimizers achieve the same data efficiency in the easy-task regime, but SignSGD maintains this efficiency at larger batch sizes, requiring fewer optimization steps for a fixed data budget. Power-law kernel regression experiments support the proposed mechanism and predicted scaling behavior. LLM pre-training experiments further suggest that the SignSGD FSL better captures the batch-size dependence of loss dynamics for sign-based optimizers than the original SGD FSL.
